title: Fascism, Gandhism and Feminism

cards.h: Three very different ideologies in one lesson
cards.b:
The syllabus lists three ideologies together: Fascism, Gandhism and Feminism. They share little. Fascism worships the nation-state and the leader. Gandhism trusts moral force and small communities. Feminism asks how gender shapes power.

Each is a regular source of questions, and the three together suit comparative questions. Learn one clear definition, key thinkers with books and years, and one critique for each.

Gandhi's ideas are covered in depth in lesson 0-8-3, so here we treat him as an ideology. For fascism, the aim is to define it precisely and to distinguish it from authoritarianism and communism.

Fascism arose in Europe between the world wars, in Italy under Benito Mussolini (in power from the March on Rome, 1922) and in Germany under Hitler (Chancellor, 1933). The word comes from the Latin fasces, a bundle of rods with an axe, a Roman symbol of authority.

  • Ultra-nationalism: the nation, often a race, is supreme.
  • Anti-individualism: the individual is nothing apart from the nation.
  • Leader principle: the Duce or Fuhrer embodies the nation.
  • Struggle and militarism: war is noble and purifying.
  • Anti-liberalism, anti-communism, anti-rationalism: it prefers will, myth and action to reason.
  • Corporatism: classes are merged into state-run bodies, so no class struggle.

Mussolini's slogan: everything within the state, nothing outside it, nothing against it.

cards.h: Fascist thought and the totalitarian state
cards.b:
Mussolini and Gentile, The Doctrine of Fascism (1932)

The philosopher Giovanni Gentile wrote the first part; Mussolini signed it. It rejects liberalism, socialism and pacifism and glorifies the state.

Hitler, Mein Kampf (1925-26)

Nazism added racial theory: the "Aryan" race against Jews, Slavs and others. The Holocaust murdered about six million Jews.

Hannah Arendt, The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951)

Total rule uses terror and ideology to dominate every part of life. She links it to anti-Semitism, imperialism and the isolated masses.

Umberto Eco, "Ur-Fascism" (1995)

Lists fourteen typical features, such as the cult of tradition, fear of difference and a permanent enemy.

cards.h: Why fascism rose, and what it is not
cards.b:
• Causes: shock of World War I, the Great Depression, fear of communism, humiliation after Versailles (Germany) and weak democracy.
  • Marxist view (Dimitrov, 1935): fascism is the open dictatorship of finance capital. Others stress the middle classes, mass politics and propaganda.
  • Robert Paxton, The Anatomy of Fascism (2004): study what fascists do, in stages from movement to rule, not just what they say.

It differs from communism (which claims class equality) and from ordinary authoritarianism, because fascism mobilises the masses in a party movement. Defeat in 1945 ended the regimes, but "neo-fascist" and far-right movements persist, and the label is much debated.

cards.h: Gandhism: a way of life as a politics
cards.b:
Gandhism is a moral and political philosophy of M.K. Gandhi (1869-1948), not a formal system. Its core is the unity of means and ends: good ends need pure means.

In Hind Swaraj (1909), Gandhi attacked modern industrial civilisation. He saw it as materialist, violent and unjust, and he pointed to the railways, lawyers and machinery as signs of this. Swaraj meant more than self-rule. It was self-rule over oneself, and a society built from self-governing villages.

He drew on the Bhagavad Gita, Jain and Buddhist ahimsa, Tolstoy, Ruskin's Unto This Last (which he turned into Sarvodaya) and Thoreau.

Gandhi's methods of satyagraha include non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting and boycott. Examples: Champaran (1917), the Salt March (1930) and Quit India (1942). The constructive programme (khadi, village industry, removing untouchability, communal unity, education) is the social side.

On the state, he was a philosophical anarchist: the ideal is an "enlightened anarchy" with minimal state power and decentralised units, like "oceanic circles" of villages.

• Impractical: critics say a modern state needs industry, defence and large institutions.
  • Ambedkar saw the village as a "sink of localism" and a "den of ignorance", where caste rules (his speech in the Constituent Assembly, 1948). He also disputed Gandhi on varna.
  • Marxists: trusteeship asks capitalists to give up power voluntarily. It hides class conflict.
  • Feminists say his ideas on women's roles were limited, though women joined his movements in large numbers.

Relevance: Gandhian ideas shaped Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela and civil resistance movements. They inform debates on environment (limits to consumption, Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful, 1973), peace and local self-government.

Feminism is the movement and theory that studies women's subordination and seeks to end it. Key terms: sex (biological) versus gender (social roles), and patriarchy (rule by men, in family and state). Its slogan, "the personal is political", says that private life, like housework and violence at home, is a matter of power.

The "wave" scheme is a rough guide, and critics note that it leaves out many movements outside the West.

Liberal

Equal rights and opportunity within the existing system: vote, education, work. Wollstonecraft, Mill, Friedan, and Okin's later work on the family.

Marxist and socialist

Women's oppression comes from capitalism and private property. Engels, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884). Socialist feminists add patriarchy to class (unpaid domestic labour).

Radical

Patriarchy is the root. It must be uprooted in family, sexuality and culture. Millett, Sexual Politics (1970); Firestone, The Dialectic of Sex (1970).

Black, postcolonial and postmodern

See next card.

• Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792): women appear weak because they are denied education.
  • J.S. Mill, The Subjection of Women (1869): legal subjection of women is a wrong.
  • Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex (1949): "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." Woman is treated as the "Other".
  • Betty Friedan, The Feminine Mystique (1963): the "problem that has no name" among American housewives.
  • Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989): coined intersectionality. Black women face overlapping race and gender discrimination.
  • Judith Butler, Gender Trouble (1990): gender is performed, not natural.
  • Chandra Mohanty: warns against treating "Third World woman" as one victim category ("Under Western Eyes", boundary 2, 1984).

cards.h: Fascism, Gandhism and feminism in India
cards.b:
• Feminism: reformers like Savitribai Phule and Jyotirao Phule (girls' school, Pune, 1848), Pandita Ramabai, Tarabai Shinde (Stri Purush Tulana, 1882) and Begum Rokeya (Sultana's Dream, 1905). Laws: sati abolition (1829), Widow Remarriage Act (1856), Hindu Code Bills (1955-56). Constitution: Article 15(3), Article 14, and Article 39(a) and (d). Vishaka (1997) led to the POSH Act (2013). The 106th Amendment (2023) reserves a third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats for women.
  • Courts: Shayara Bano (2017) struck down instant triple talaq; Joseph Shine (2018) struck down adultery law; Indian Young Lawyers Association (2018) opened Sabarimala to women.
  • Gandhism: Sarvodaya and Bhoodan (Vinoba Bhave, 1951), Panchayati Raj and Article 40, khadi, and Chipko.
  • Fascism: Gandhi wrote to Hitler in 1939 and 1940. The Constitution's rights, secular state and independent judiciary are safeguards against totalitarian rule.

"Fascism is the negation of liberal democracy." Discuss.
Examine Gandhi's critique of modern civilisation and its relevance today.
Explain the various strands of feminism.
Is Gandhi's concept of trusteeship a feasible alternative to socialism?

Structure: for fascism, define it, give six features, then thinkers (Mussolini, Arendt) and causes. For Gandhi, start from Hind Swaraj and give means-ends, satyagraha, sarvodaya and trusteeship, then critics (Ambedkar, Marxists) and relevance. For feminism, give the waves, the schools and one Indian example for each. Close with a comparison table, if the question asks for it.

quiz.q: The Doctrine of Fascism (1932) was signed by Mussolini; the philosopher who wrote its first part was…
The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951) is by…
quiz.w: Arendt analysed Nazi and Stalinist totalitarianism.

o: Merge classes into state-run bodies and end class struggle
quiz.w: It replaced class conflict with state-controlled corporations.
Gandhi wrote it in 1909 on a ship from England to South Africa.

quiz.q: Gandhi's Sarvodaya was inspired by Ruskin's…
o: The Kingdom of God Is Within You
quiz.w: Gandhi rendered it as Sarvodaya in Gujarati.

o: Owners of wealth hold it as trustees for society
quiz.w: Wealth is held in trust for the community.

quiz.q: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' appears in…
Radical feminists such as Millett locate the root of oppression in…
quiz.w: Sexual Politics (1970) treats patriarchy as the base system of power.

quiz.q: Which Supreme Court ruling led to the guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace in 1997?
quiz.w: Vishaka (1997); the POSH Act followed in 2013.
